outcome: The value of Λ is still not determined as of 11 Oct 2026. Λ ≥ 0 stands from Rodgers and Tao (2018), and the upper bound moved from 0.22 (Polymath15, 2019) to 0.2 (Platt and Trudgian, 2020) and then through a cluster of unrefereed 2026 claims, the lowest unconditional one being Λ < 0.149396 (Raymond, Zenodo, 21 Sep 2026). Two unrefereed preprints claim RH and hence Λ = 0 (Gershon, Apr 2026; Pavesi, Jun 2026); neither was engaged with publicly in anything I found.
problem_asks: (a) The exact real value of Λ, the de Bruijn–Newman constant: the threshold t such that all zeros of the heat-flow deformation H_t of Riemann's xi function are real exactly when t ≥ Λ. That is the whole ask, a single number. Any interval [a, b] containing Λ is a partial answer that does not state the value. The statement does not ask for a proof of RH, but background that predates the window fixes the frame: Λ ≥ 0 (Rodgers–Tao 2018), and RH is equivalent to Λ ≤ 0, so the value is 0 exactly when RH holds.

events.what_happened: N. G. de Bruijn showed Λ ≤ 1/2, the first upper bound on the constant. Recorded from the English Wikipedia article, which I opened and which attributes the bound to de Bruijn (1950). The 1950 paper itself was not opened.
events.remains: The exact value of Λ, and everything below 1/2.
events.time_since_posted: not applicable (1950); later bounds built on it
events.direction: Upper side only. Moves the trivial bound to 1/2. Consistent with RH but does not settle it.

events.what_happened: Csordas, Odlyzko, Smith and Varga gave a lower bound −5.895·10⁻⁹ < Λ, using a close pair of zeros (a Lehmer pair). Seen only in a search summary; the 1993 paper was not opened (the ETNA URL appeared in results, unopened).
events.delivers: Λ > −5.895·10⁻⁹ (lower side only).
events.doubts: Figure taken from a search summary, not from the paper.
events.direction: Lower side. Keeps Λ possibly negative, which Rodgers–Tao later excluded.

events.what_happened: Odlyzko (Numerical Algorithms 25 (2000) 293–303, per a search summary) gives −2.7·10⁻⁹ < Λ, from a pair of zeros near the 10²⁰th. A search summary says a later Rodgers–Tao table lists −2.63·10⁻⁹ for the same result; I could not resolve that. Not opened (search snippet only).
events.delivers: Λ > −2.7·10⁻⁹ (lower side only).
events.doubts: Figure −2.7 vs −2.63 ·10⁻⁹ disagrees between two sources; not resolved.
events.direction: Lower side; superseded by Rodgers–Tao's Λ ≥ 0.

events.what_happened: Ki, Kim and Lee sharpened de Bruijn's bound to Λ < 1/2 (Adv. Math. 222 (2009) 281–306). Wikipedia dates the result to 2008, probably the preprint. ScienceDirect returned 403, so the paper was not opened; the claim comes from Wikipedia, the Polymath15 paper and Rodgers–Tao as summarised in search.
events.delivers: Λ < 1/2 (strict).
events.direction: Upper side. Sharpens 1/2 to a strict inequality; still consistent with RH.

events.what_happened: Saouter, Gourdon and Demichel found a new Lehmer pair and gave Λ > −1.14541·10⁻¹¹ (Math. Comp. 80 (2011), per search summary). The AMS page returned 403 and was not opened.
events.delivers: Λ > −1.14541·10⁻¹¹ (lower side only).
events.directly_checkable: The Lehmer-pair zeros are checkable numerically; not checked here.
events.direction: Lower side; superseded by Rodgers–Tao (Λ ≥ 0).

events.what_happened: Xiao-Jun Yang posted arXiv:2211.17269 (8 Nov 2022) claiming that a function M_ℵ(τ) has only purely imaginary zeros for every real ℵ, and that 'this implies that the conjecture of Newman is true', i.e. Λ ≥ 0, which Rodgers and Tao had already proved in 2018. Opened the abstract page only.
events.delivers: Claims Λ ≥ 0 by way of a different family M_ℵ. The abstract page does not show how M_ℵ relates to H_t.
events.remains: Upper side and the value, which are untouched by this claim.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years; no engagement found in this run
events.doubts: Lower side only, and that side was already settled in 2018. The abstract does not establish the link from M_ℵ to H_t. I did not find a journal version or review in this run.
events.direction: Lower side. Claims the already-known non-negativity by a new route.

events.what_happened: Brad Rodgers and Terence Tao proved Newman's conjecture, Λ ≥ 0, in arXiv:1801.05914 (first submitted 18 Jan 2018; v5 3 Jul 2021). Published in Forum of Mathematics, Pi 8 (2020), e6, per search summary. Tao announced it on his blog (19 Jan 2018, from search results).
events.delivers: Λ ≥ 0, so the value is Λ ∈ [0, upper bound] and RH holds iff Λ = 0.
events.remains: The value Λ, i.e. whether Λ = 0.

checked_by.who: Forum of Mathematics, Pi (refereed journal, Cambridge University Press)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; refereed by its editors
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper in 2020 (vol. 8, e6), per search summary

events.direction: Lower side. Proves the non-negativity that Newman conjectured; combined with RH ⇔ Λ ≤ 0 it reduces the open question to Λ = 0.

events.what_happened: The Polymath15 collaboration (led by Terence Tao) gave an effective approximation to the heat flow of the Riemann xi function and an unconditional bound Λ ≤ 0.22 (arXiv:1904.12438, v1 29 Apr 2019; v2 4 Aug 2019; 'to appear, Research in the Mathematical Sciences'). The bound was first reported in the project's blog threads in 2018; Wikipedia dates the improvement to Dec 2018. The blog threads were not opened (polymathprojects.org returned 404 and the tagteam mirror 503), so the 2018 date rests on Wikipedia alone.
events.revisions: Blog threads 2018 (ninth thread on going below 0.22); arXiv v1 29 Apr 2019; v2 4 Aug 2019.
events.delivers: Λ ≤ 0.22, unconditional (per the arXiv abstract).

checked_by.who: The Polymath15 participants, in open blog threads run by Terence Tao; the final paper went to Research in the Mathematical Sciences
checked_by.qualification: Mathematicians working in the project in public, with open review of the threads
checked_by.what_they_did: Public discussion of the arguments and numerical checks across the blog threads; the arXiv paper is the written record

events.time_since_posted: about 7 years for the arXiv version
events.directly_checkable: Numerical verification of H_t zero-freeness in the stated regions, code in the public km-git-acc/dbn_upper_bound repository (not run).
events.direction: Upper side. Moves the upper bound from 1/2 to 0.22.

events.what_happened: Alexander Dobner gave a second proof of Newman's conjecture (Λ ≥ 0) that needs no information about the zeros of ζ, and extended it to L-functions in the extended Selberg class (arXiv:2005.05142, v1 11 May 2020; v2 10 Jan 2026; Acta Arithmetica 201 (2021) 29–62). Opened the arXiv abstract page only.
events.delivers: Λ ≥ 0 by a new route; for every L-function in the extended Selberg class the analogous constant is non-negative.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, Acta Arith. 201 (2021), 29–62 (per arXiv metadata; not opened)

events.direction: Lower side only; confirms Rodgers–Tao's result by another method.

events.what_happened: David Platt and Timothy Trudgian verified rigorously that all zeros β+iγ of ζ with 0 < γ ≤ 3·10¹² have β = 1/2 (arXiv:2004.09765, first submitted 21 Apr 2020). Combined with the Polymath15 criterion this gives Λ ≤ 0.2; Wikipedia states this as 'slightly improved in April 2020 by Platt and Trudgian to Λ ≤ 0.2'. Published in the Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 53(3) (2021), doi 10.1112/blms.12460. The PDF returned binary and was not readable here; the Λ ≤ 0.2 step is taken from Wikipedia and a search summary of §3.4, not read directly.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only; journal Bull. LMS 53(3) (2021).
events.delivers: Finite RH verification to height 3·10¹² (the verified height is the input the 0.2 bound uses). Per Wikipedia, Λ ≤ 0.2 via the Polymath15 criterion.

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, 53(3), 2021 (per DOI and arXiv metadata; not opened)

events.directly_checkable: The height verification is a finite computation; the program was not inspected.
events.direction: Upper side. Moves the upper bound from 0.22 to 0.2.

events.what_happened: Raghu Raj Shree posted 'Analysis of the De Bruijn–Newman Constant and Its Implications for the Riemann Hypothesis' on OSF Preprints (DOI 10.31219/osf.io/d6hm4), 22 Oct 2024. The abstract, per OpenAlex, analyses the integral H(0,z) and an associated series Φ(u), and reports H(0,z) ≠ 0 for all real and complex z, which 'suggests Λ ≠ 0' and that RH may not hold. The OSF page returned no readable content; the abstract is from the OpenAlex inverted index.
events.delivers: Claims H(0,z) ≠ 0 for all complex z, and so Λ ≠ 0 and RH false (per the abstract as reconstructed).
events.remains: The value; the paper claims to decide against Λ = 0.
events.directly_checkable: If H(0,·) is the standard Ξ = H_0, the claim is checkable against the known zeros of ξ, which would make it false.
events.doubts: The claim H(0,z) ≠ 0 for all complex z conflicts with the known zeros of Ξ, if H(0,·) is the standard H_0 = Ξ; I could not read the paper's definition of H(0,·) to check. Author has no listed affiliation. OpenAlex's concept tags include mis-tags ('Programming language', 'Constant (computer programming)').
events.direction: Cuts against RH (and so against Λ = 0), if its claim holds.

events.what_happened: Castillo, Muñoz, Poblete and Salinas posted 'The Generalized Riemann Zeta heat flow' (arXiv:2402.10154, 15 Feb 2024): PDE flows for ζ and Dirichlet L-functions, with local/global existence and blow-up. It is motivated by the backward heat equation that Λ satisfies, per search summary of the introduction (not read). The abstract page does not mention Λ.
events.delivers: PDE results for a zeta heat flow. No bound on Λ and no value of Λ.
events.direction: Not about Λ; discarded. Different question (PDE flow for ζ).

events.what_happened: Wojciech Michalowski posted arXiv:2602.20313 (first submitted 23 Feb 2026): the de Bruijn–Newman kernel is not a Pólya frequency function of order 5, via an interval certificate at one configuration. Version 2 withdraws the certified global sign and unique-threshold claims for C₅, because a derivative-tail enclosure was unsound. The paper says it 'does not resolve the Riemann Hypothesis' and does not concern Λ.
events.revisions: v1 23 Feb 2026; v2 withdraws the global sign and unique-threshold claims for C₅ (v2 date not read).
events.delivers: Total positivity (PF order) of the kernel. Says nothing about the zeros of H_t or about Λ.
events.remains: All of the question about Λ.
events.directly_checkable: The interval certificate was not checked.
events.doubts: The author's own v2 withdraws part of v1.

withdrawn.what: v1 claims of a certified global sign and unique threshold for C₅ (derivative-tail enclosure unsound)

events.direction: Not about Λ; discarded. A different question about the kernel's total positivity.
events.object: The kernel itself, at one configuration, is shown not to be PF5 by an interval-arithmetic certificate (per the abstract as read). Explicit as a certificate, not a construction of a new object.

events.what_happened: Avi Gershon posted 'The De Bruijn–Newman Constant Is Zero' on Preprints.org (DOI 10.20944/preprints202604.1513.v1), 22 Apr 2026. The abstract (via PREreview; the Preprints.org page returned 403) claims: strict log-concavity of a 'Riemann–Jacobi kernel'; hyperbolicity of certain Jensen polynomials for small degrees and indices; that global RH is algebraically equivalent to a 'subluminal' condition on Wronskian components; kernel negativity for x ≥ 0 and for negative x 'in a range of degrees and indices verified by interval-arithmetic computation'; and that a spectral-gap argument, certified numerics and Borell log-concavity establish RH unconditionally and Λ = 0.
events.delivers: Claims Λ = 0 (equivalently RH). If correct it settles the problem at the value 0.
events.time_since_posted: about 5.5 months; no reviews or comments on the PREreview page; none found elsewhere in this run
events.directly_checkable: The interval-arithmetic certificates (dissipation bound and degree/index range) would be checkable; not read.
events.doubts: (1) The abstract itself says negativity for negative x is verified only 'for a range of degrees and indices'. A finite range is not a proof for all degrees. (2) A third-party survey (BitConcepts riemann-solver, LANDSCAPE.md) states that the final step needs a dissipation bound S ≤ 19.41 that rests on a 10,822-point interval-arithmetic computation, and records the status as NOT peer-reviewed. (3) The survey says a companion log-concavity preprint's perturbation bound 'goes the wrong direction'. (4) No expert engagement found.
events.direction: Cuts toward Λ = 0, i.e. toward RH being true, if the claim holds.
people: Avi Gershon (affiliation not stated on the page)

events.what_happened: Luca Eliseo Pavesi posted 'A Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis via the Log-Concavity of the Pólya Kernel' on Zenodo (record 20806677, CC BY 4.0). The record shown is v5, publication date 23 Jun 2026; earlier versions were not examined. The abstract claims 'We prove the Riemann Hypothesis by establishing the log-concavity of the Pólya kernel'. The landing page does not mention Λ or de Bruijn–Newman.
events.revisions: Zenodo v5 (23 Jun 2026) shown; a newer record version exists per the page; earlier versions not examined.
events.delivers: Claims RH. RH is equivalent to Λ ≤ 0, so together with Λ ≥ 0 this would give Λ = 0. The paper itself does not state the Λ consequence, as far as the landing page shows.
events.doubts: A single-author Zenodo preprint claiming a proof of RH, with no review or engagement found. Only the landing page was read; the full PDF was not.
events.direction: Cuts toward Λ = 0 (RH) if the claim holds.

events.what_happened: 'Mosaic Intelligence' (no affiliation listed) posted 'A certified unconditional upper bound Λ ≤ 0.1965 for the de Bruijn–Newman constant' on Zenodo (record 20724170, v1), publication date 17 Jun 2026. Abstract: 'Subject to the published Polymath15 criterion and the published Platt–Trudgian verification, the attached certificates prove, unconditionally, Λ ≤ 0.1965 = 1965/10000 exactly'. Superseded by v2 (see next event). The landing page names no AI system; its only AI-related item is the keyword 'AI-generated mathematics'.
events.revisions: v1 17 Jun 2026 (Λ ≤ 0.1965); superseded by v2 3 Jul 2026 (Λ ≤ 3/16).
events.delivers: Λ ≤ 0.1965 given the published Polymath15 criterion and Platt–Trudgian verification; the author describes it as unconditional, meaning not dependent on RH.
events.time_since_posted: about 4 months; no engagement found on the record
events.directly_checkable: Certificates in the Zenodo record (not downloaded).
events.doubts: Author identity unknown ('Mosaic Intelligence', no affiliation). Superseded by the author's own v2.
events.direction: Upper side. Moves the upper bound from 0.2 to 0.1965 (claimed).
people: Mosaic Intelligence (creator name; no human named)

events.what_happened: The same 'Mosaic Intelligence' posted v2 of the certified bound, 'A certified unconditional upper bound Λ ≤ 0.1875 for the de Bruijn–Newman constant' (Zenodo record 21175533, published 3 Jul 2026): Λ ≤ 3/16 = 0.1875 exactly, on the same conditional basis (published Polymath15 criterion and Platt–Trudgian verification), verified 'on two mechanically independent code lines'. The Zenodo abstract says: 'This is a fully AI-derived body of results, as disclosed in the paper.' The paper PDF (main.pdf, 239.7 kB) returned binary and was not readable, so the disclosure sentence in the paper itself was not read and no system is named.
events.delivers: Λ ≤ 3/16 = 0.1875, claimed unconditional given the published Polymath15 criterion and the Platt–Trudgian verification.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 months. A computo ergo sum critique (10 Sep 2026) refers to 'Mosaic's Zenodo version' but I did not confirm any reviewer.
events.directly_checkable: Certificate archive dbn21a-certificates.zip (196.2 MB) on the Zenodo record; not downloaded.
events.doubts: Author identity unknown. The paper states the work is 'fully AI-derived' but the model is not named in any page I could read. The bound is cited by the computo ergo sum critique as the base of the 0.1787854 proof (see disputes).

people: Mosaic Intelligence (creator name; no human named)

events.what_happened: Jude Gomila (sole listed author; 'special thanks to Dan Romik and Max Atkin') publishes a computer-assisted proof that Λ ≤ 893927/5000000 = 0.1787854, as the GitHub repository judegomila/dbn-lambda-01787854-candidate-audit (earliest visible commit 28 Jul 2026: 'Release sealed referee snapshot for Lambda <= 0.1787854 (v3)'; 29 commits to 21 Aug 2026) and a blog post dated 19 Aug 2026. The proof combines the Polymath15 criterion (Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:1904.12438) and the Platt–Trudgian verified height with three hypotheses: (i) no zeros up to height X/2 (X = 6,000,000,185,827), (ii) final-time clearance by about 3.15 million interval-certified windows plus a tail lemma, (iii) a barrier over 0 ≤ t ≤ t₀ = 129/800 checked by 883 time prisms and the argument principle. Certificates are fail-closed interval-arithmetic (FLINT/Arb). The author says the bound 'does not assume RH and is not a proof of RH'. The repository's release manuscript has a human–AI collaboration disclosure (see ai). Status: 'not yet peer reviewed'; 'journal publication is the remaining step'. The date recorded is the earliest visible public commit; whether the repository was publicly visible on that day was not checked, and earlier snapshots (v1, v2) are referenced but not in the visible history.
events.revisions: Repository: 29 visible commits, 28 Jul – 21 Aug 2026; referee snapshot 'v3'. Blog post 19 Aug 2026. Release manuscript dated 20 Aug 2026 (per repo). Lean lemma layer 20 Aug 2026 (per repo README). Replay issue #31 opened 5 Oct 2026, still open.
events.delivers: Λ ≤ 0.1787854, claimed unconditional given the published Polymath15 Theorem 1.2 and the Platt–Trudgian verified height. The repository and author both say it is not a proof of RH. Per the repository's own referee report, the verified height must be the precise value 3 000 175 332 800; the rounded '3×10¹²' would make hypothesis (i) fail.
events.remains: Λ ∈ [0, 0.1787854] if the claim holds; the value.

checked_by.who: Dan Romik (named by the author as 'independent reviewer'; the repo's 'dan-reworking/' folder is 'the referee's in-progress reworking', marked 'Not attested'; the repo does not say Romik is that referee)
checked_by.qualification: A mathematician who has published on the Riemann xi function (arXiv:1902.06330, 'Orthogonal polynomial expansions for the Riemann xi function') and is credited with the independent programs in the repo

checked_by.what_they_did: Reviewed each proof leg on 28 Jul 2026. Found no fatal or bound-invalidating defect in an adversarial pass; flagged the Dini y-transfer inequality (worst ratio 0.99999860767275095) as 'the one real gap' (not executed or log-audited by the sealed assembly), and two prose-only analytic steps (B_t ≠ 0 on the rectangle R; the t>0 to t=0 extension of Lemma 8.4 / Theorem 1.3). Verdict: the package 'may not yet advance beyond unreviewed computer-assisted proof candidate'. Addendum (same day): recompiled the heavy computations and reproduced the certified bounds; residual is 'purely human-mathematician analytic sign-off'.

checked_by.who: Vichien Fugsukjit, independent researcher, Bangkok (GitHub issue #31, opened 5 Oct 2026, still open)
checked_by.qualification: Independent replayer; used AI-assisted tooling (Claude) per the issue text
checked_by.what_they_did: Reproducibility only. Ran verify.sh (PASS; SHA-256 seal 443 files) and three non-container replays (PASS). Did not referee the mathematics. Found a seal failure on Windows clones with core.autocrlf=true; suggested .gitattributes fixes.

checked_by.qualification: Automated verification by the site's AI; no named mathematician

States the verifiers confirm completeness and minimum margin, 'not that each of the 3,149,013 rows is correct'; the independent cross-check of the finite-lane algorithm was not run (more than a day). Concludes 'There is no new mathematics in this article'.

checked_by.who: Michel Planat (Institut FEMTO-ST, CNRS UMR 6174, Besançon)
checked_by.what_they_did: Uses the Gomila package only as 'the numerical producer for the three hypotheses'. States that 'The global numerical conclusion remains an audit-relative candidate bound until that numerical input and its weld to the published criterion receive independent mathematical review.' This is use, not endorsement.

events.time_since_posted: about 7 weeks since the blog post (19 Aug 2026); about 11 weeks since the first visible commit (28 Jul 2026)

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with mathlib (v4.22.0 and v4.28.0), lemma layer only; the Aristotle-generated files state they are 'sorry-free' with standard axioms; the Lean theorem assumes the Arb-certified numerics and the argument principle as explicit hypotheses

events.directly_checkable: The certificate set: 3,149,013 window certificates, 883 barrier prisms and one tail certificate (per the repo header), run by verify.sh with FLINT/Arb. Reproducible from the repository on Linux (per issue #31); Windows clones need core.autocrlf=false.
events.doubts: (1) The referee report's Dini y-transfer inequality was not executed by the sealed assembly at first (addendum says it was later wired in). (2) Two analytic steps are prose-only (B_t ≠ 0 on R; the t>0 to t=0 extension), and the Lean layer covers only 'reduction logic' with the two candidate-specific hypotheses 'NOT proved here' (lean/BarrierAnalyticSkeleton.lean). (3) The repo's own README says the Lean theorem 'is conditional on' the Arb-certified numerics. (4) The fast verifiers parse printed enclosures rather than recompute them (addendum says this was closed by recompile). (5) Sensitivity to the exact Platt–Trudgian height (rounding to 3×10¹² breaks hypothesis (i)). (6) The critique's claim that the bound 'builds on Mosaic's 0.1875' conflicts with the blog post's framing 'from 0.2 to 0.1787854' (see disputes). (7) No journal submission is recorded in the sources.
events.direction: Upper side. Narrows the window from 0.2 (or the Mosaic 0.1875) to 0.1787854, claimed unconditional. It is not a value and does not reach 0 or RH.
people: Dan Romik (named as independent reviewer; no own statement found)

events.what_happened: A computer-assisted 'collision-exclusion' method by Kornaus is reported to give Λ < 0.172422, using a moving separator, a mollified real-double-zero resultant, transport across Riemann–Siegel cutoff changes and an explicit tail theorem. I could not find Kornaus's own paper: five searches returned no source. The only description is Planat's arXiv:2609.37164 v2 (7 Oct 2026), which cites it as reference [7] and imports the band [0.172422, 0.2] as 'an imported computational input'.
events.delivers: Per Planat's description only: Λ < 0.172422 by a computer-assisted method. Not read at source.
events.remains: The value; and the interval [0, 0.172422] is a claim, not a checked result.
events.doubts: Source not located. Planat's own work says the band is imported and 'require[s] independent mathematical review'. The search summary of Planat also says the Kornaus method's 'separator and frozen-cutoff remainder interfaces' need review.
events.direction: Upper side, if the description is right.

events.what_happened: Stefan Gordon posted 'A computer-assisted upper bound for the de Bruijn–Newman constant' (GitHub stefangordon/dbn-upper-bound): Λ ≤ 3885632262767861213460393068710302759 / 24646172707879668706230182733520000000, decimal 0.157656619095490606768… < 0.158. It combines the Platt–Trudgian finite-RH theorem with new analytic estimates (Appendix A) and rigorous interval computations (Appendix C). The repo says 'The paper has not undergone external peer review'. Month of first public posting is 'September 2026' per the repo's PROVENANCE.md ('initial research and drafts were produced in September 2026') and Planat's reference list; the repo shows 8 commits and no dates.
events.delivers: Λ ≤ 0.157656619… (< 0.158), claimed. Conditional: 'The Lean theorem is conditional on explicit analytic inputs; this is not a complete formal proof of the numerical bound.'
events.remains: Λ ∈ [0, 0.1577]; the value. The analytic inputs are conditional in the Lean layer.
events.time_since_posted: about 1–2 months; no engagement beyond citation (Planat v2)

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (partial; lake build per the repo's lean/README.md)

PROVENANCE says a 'GPT-6 Astra' reviewer and a 'Claude Code' assistant were used (see ai). A search summary of Planat's v2 (unread text) gives the endpoint as approximately 0.1576566, consistent with the repo.

events.what_happened: Michel Planat posted arXiv:2609.37164, 'Collective Contraction in the de Bruijn–Newman Heat Flow: Off-Zero Logarithmic Derivatives and Certified Barrier Refinements' (v1 29 Sep 2026; v2 7 Oct 2026 with a new Section 6 hybrid extension, per the introduction). Read v2's first 100,000 characters of the HTML. What I read: an 'audit-relative endpoint' Λ ≤ 0.177953254642861… from Gomila's package, Corollary 4.3 (Λ < 0.177954, audit-relative), and a conditional hybrid Λ < 0.16836 (Section 6). The introduction imports Kornaus's band [0.172422, 0.2] and cites Gordon [8] and Raymond [9]. From search summaries of later text I could not read directly: a higher-order continuation of Gordon's density–jet barrier giving a candidate Λ ≤ 64356644694133/408948000000000 < 0.157371218, which the paper says is a conditional sector landing and 'not, by itself, a global upper bound'; and a reproduction of Raymond's endpoint. Those later parts must be verified against the paper.
events.revisions: v1 29 Sep 2026 (16 KB); v2 7 Oct 2026 (54 pages, 'big expansion'); v2 adds Section 6 hybrid per the introduction.
events.delivers: Conditional and audit-relative bounds only: 0.177953 (on Gomila's package), 0.16836 (hybrid, conditional on explicit interfaces). The 0.157371 candidate is, per the summary, conditional and not a global bound on its own.
events.remains: The value of Λ. The paper treats Λ as undetermined and its endpoints as candidates.

The paper says 'the assembled upper bound remains conditional on the explicit source-to-theorem interfaces'. The paper calls the Gomila base 'publicly replayable but not yet peer-reviewed'.

events.what_happened: Dale James Raymond posted 'Correlated translated probes and the bound Λ < 0.149396 for the de Bruijn–Newman constant' (Zenodo record 22867547, published 21 Sep 2026; GitHub Dale-Dug/de-bruijn-newman-0149396, 'Version 1.0'). Bound: Λ ≤ 18674384228461/125000000000000 = 0.149395073827688 < 0.149396. Method per the repo: the classical time-zero strip, a finite-head localisation wall, uniform logarithmic-derivative estimates and 'correlated translated-probe zero motion'. The repo says 'This positive upper-bound claim is not a proof of the Riemann hypothesis or of Λ < 0.09' (the second number as printed). Only the Zenodo landing page and repo description were read; the full PDF was not.
events.revisions: Zenodo record single version v1 (21 Sep 2026); repo labels it Version 1.0.
events.delivers: Λ < 0.149396 (claimed; the page does not state a hypothesis, so it is read as unconditional).
events.time_since_posted: about 3 weeks; 'has not undergone external peer review' (Zenodo)
events.directly_checkable: The repo's 'exact rational final comparisons' (Arb/FLINT); not run here.
events.doubts: 'Not formally verified end to end' (repo). The repo says the analytic arguments and proof-to-code correspondence 'need human review'. The repo's 'Λ < 0.09' phrase is unexplained. Planat's v2 reportedly reproduces the endpoint numerically (search summary; not read).
events.direction: Upper side, claimed. The lowest unconditional upper bound I found.

events.what_happened: OpenAI published the openai/math repository of manuscripts 'produced by an internal OpenAI model' (722 manuscripts in 372 families per the README; one source says 719). It includes a 'zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function' with writeup 'for the Re(s) > 11/12 zero-free region', 'human edited for readability'. The README lists the zero-free region as an exception to the repo's fixed procedure. The README does not mention Λ, de Bruijn or Newman. Press reports date the release to 6 Oct 2026. Quoted here from the README at raw.githubusercontent.com, which I opened.
events.revisions: The README says: 'Corrections and revisions will be recorded as new versions, with previously released versions remaining accessible.' Repo shows 3 commits. A third-party repo cites commit adc7f124 with a 7/8 theorem (see disputes).
events.delivers: A zero-free region for ζ(s) in Re(s) > 11/12 (per the current README). Does not by itself give a bound on Λ. Any bound on Λ from it requires a conversion made by others (see the next event).
events.time_since_posted: 5 days; the README says results 'are at different stages of verification' and not all have Lean formalisations; no peer review
events.directly_checkable: Lean formalisations exist for part of the collection (README; press reports about 42% of top-line results, not verified); the 9/32 repo says it replayed the 7/8 theorem through Comparator.
events.doubts: Unrefereed. Version discrepancy: the README states Re(s) > 11/12, while the 9/32 repo cites a theorem named for 7/8 (see disputes). A press summary (not opened) says some items were retracted after outside mistakes were found; not verified.
events.direction: Concerns zeros of ζ, not Λ. Relevant to Λ only through a conversion by a third party (next event).
people: OpenAI (no named human author in the README)

events.what_happened: Peter W. Murphy (GitHub DrMurphyIsIn) released 'A kernel-checked bound Lambda <= 9/32 for the de Bruijn-Newman constant from OpenAI's quasi-Riemann hypothesis' (Zenodo 23269135, v1.0.0, 9 Oct 2026; repo qrh-debruijn-newman). Claim: 'Every zero of H_t is real for every t ≥ 9/32', i.e. Λ ≤ 9/32 ≈ 0.28125. Route: OpenAI's theorem ζ(s) ≠ 0 for Re s > 7/8 (named OAI.riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_seven_eighths_lt_re, at openai/math commit adc7f124), converted by the repo's formula Λ ≤ 2(θ − ½)² with θ = 7/8, plus de Bruijn's theorem in parametric form (formalised in the Arda project). Lean 4 composition theorem with standard axioms only, re-checked by nanoda through Comparator. The repo says 'Not RH' and 'Nothing here proves anything about ζ'.
events.revisions: Zenodo v1.0.0 9 Oct 2026; the repo's 'OpenAI release in October 2026' and audit file dated 2026-10-07 (docs/QRH_DBN_AUDIT_2026-10-07_e9.md, not read).
events.delivers: Λ ≤ 9/32 (claimed), conditional on OpenAI's zero-free-region theorem (at the 7/8 version the repo uses) and on the de Bruijn theorem. The machine-checked part is the conversion, not the zero-free region.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Comparator and nanoda (kernel re-check); axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]

events.directly_checkable: The Lean composition theorem dbn_real_zeros_of_qrh_unconditional, with its external input at openai/math commit adc7f124 (the repo says this was replayed through Comparator but not proved by the repo).
events.doubts: (1) The bound depends on OpenAI's zero-free region; the current openai/math README says Re(s) > 11/12, not 7/8. By the repo's own formula, θ = 11/12 gives 2(11/12 − 1/2)² = 25/72 ≈ 0.347 (my arithmetic), which is weaker than 9/32; this is not checked against the repo. (2) The repo says the de Bruijn half 'depends on other work'. (3) The repo's formula Λ ≤ 2(θ−½)² and the conversion are the repo's claims and were not verified here. (4) Press coverage overstates the OpenAI result as proving RH; the repo itself says 'Not RH'.
events.direction: Upper side. The bound 9/32 is weaker than Polymath15's 0.22, so it does not move the frontier; its interest is that it is kernel-checked.

events.what_happened: Dale James Raymond released a companion repository for a conditional bound Λ < 0.116398 (GitHub Dale-Dug/de-bruijn-newman-0116398; Zenodo 23272725; 'Version 1.0, 10 October 2026'). Bound: Λ ≤ 116397726408291/10¹⁵ = 0.116397726408291 < 0.116398, conditional on hypothesis H(7/8): 'every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part at most 7/8', including the boundary line. The repo says 'the numerical checks do not establish H(7/8)' and 'a conditional preprint, with no claim of an unconditional record, a proof of RH'. AI statement: 'The work was developed with AI assistance; the named author is responsible for the claims.'
events.revisions: Version 1.0, 10 Oct 2026. Relation to the 21 Sep 2026 unconditional record not stated in the pages read.
events.delivers: Λ < 0.116398 conditional on H(7/8).
events.remains: The value; and H(7/8), which the repo does not establish.
events.time_since_posted: 1 day. The repo says 'No fresh wall production or Lean execution was performed for this review'.
events.doubts: Conditional on an unproved hypothesis, by the repo's own statement. The hypothesis H(7/8) is the same hypothesis the 9/32 repo's OpenAI input is taken to establish (at the 7/8 version). Whether that input establishes H(7/8) is in dispute (see disputes).
events.direction: Upper side, conditional on H(7/8). Cuts toward Λ = 0 if H(7/8) and the numerics hold, but not established.

events.what_happened: A GitHub repository n0zer0d4y/debruijn-newman-large-sieve (MIT for code, CC BY 4.0 for papers; 'September–October 2026' literature searches) gives three results: a Λ-analogue result, that Λ is unbounded on a family of Dirichlet series sharing the functional equation of L(s, χ₋₇) (Theorem U, written proof); a certified Λ_DH > 0.23 for the Davenport–Heilbronn function (upper Λ_DH ≤ 0.58 conditional); and a prime-moduli large-sieve result. events.time_since_posted: unknown; 'No human expert has reviewed them yet'

disputes.summary: Mosaic Intelligence's Λ ≤ 3/16 = 0.1875 (Zenodo v2, 3 Jul 2026) predates Gomila's Λ ≤ 0.1787854 (repo commit 28 Jul; blog 19 Aug 2026). The computo ergo sum critique says Gomila's candidate 'is built on top of the preceding Λ ≤ 0.1875 (Mosaic)' and lists Mosaic among the sources. Gomila's blog presents the prior ceiling as 0.2 and attributes it to Polymath15 and Platt–Trudgian. I could not check the reference list of Gomila's paper, so I cannot say whether it cites Mosaic. The record does not pick a winner.

Gomila's blog says the proof received an 'independent human review by Dan Romik' and calls the pre-publication pass an 'adversarial AI review panel'. The repo file named EXTERNAL_REFEREE_REPORT_2026-07-28.md is a report by 'adversarial AI referee panel (four independent agents...), directed and synthesized by Claude (Opus 4.8)' and states it is 'not a substitute for human expert peer review'. No separate statement by Romik was found, and the repo says the Romik-associated folder is 'Not attested'. The 'external referee' label and the 'independent human review' label do not match what the files show.

The OpenAI zero-free region used by the 9/32 bound is stated as Re(s) > 7/8 in the Lean name of the 9/32 repo (commit adc7f124) but as 'the Re(s) > 11/12 zero-free region' in the current openai/math README. The repo's formula would give 9/32 at 7/8 and 25/72 ≈ 0.347 at 11/12 (my arithmetic). Either OpenAI revised the theorem, or one source is wrong. Unresolved.

The Raymond conditional bound Λ < 0.116398 is conditional on H(7/8). The OpenAI result in the 9/32 repo is the zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8, the same hypothesis in the other direction. If the 7/8 version of the OpenAI theorem held, it would give H(7/8) and make the 0.116 bound unconditional. The Raymond repo says its numerical checks do not establish H(7/8). The two sources do not address each other.

summary: The problem's value is not determined. What is established since the frozen revision: nothing new about Λ ≥ 0 (Rodgers–Tao 2018 and Dobner 2020 stand; the 2022 Yang claim restates it), and the upper bound has fallen since 26 Jan 2024 from 0.2 (Platt–Trudgian 2020, which I took from Wikipedia and a search summary of their §3.4, since their PDF was unreadable) to a cluster of 2026 claims. All of these are unrefereed preprints or repositories, and most are explicitly conditional or 'not yet peer reviewed'. The lowest unconditional figure I found is Raymond's Λ < 0.149396 (Zenodo, 21 Sep 2026), which I read only from its landing page and repository description. Next are Gordon's partly-formalised Λ ≤ 0.157656… (Sept 2026, conditional on analytic inputs in its Lean layer), Gomila's Λ ≤ 0.1787854 (repo 28 Jul, blog 19 Aug 2026), and Mosaic's 3/16 (3 Jul 2026, the PDF unreadable). Two events sit at a different level: Gomila's bound is the most publicised, with a replay (issue #31) and an AI-run critique that both confirm the computation but not the mathematics. Its 'independent human review' is, on the files, an AI panel plus an unpublished claim by Dan Romik that I could not confirm, and the release disclosure names Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex as used across exploration, program development, testing and revision. The Lean layer (Harmonic Aristotle, per the repo's notes) formalises the reduction logic and assumes the numerics as hypotheses; I have not counted it as AI in ai.systems because it formalises rather than produces mathematics, but the later pass should weigh it. The 9/32 repo (9 Oct 2026) is kernel-checked and built on an OpenAI-produced zero-free region, which the openai/math README now gives as Re(s) > 11/12, not 7/8: the claim depends on which version is right. Planat's arXiv:2609.37164 (v2, 7 Oct 2026) is the citing hub for Kornaus (0.172422, which I could not locate), Gordon and Raymond; its headline numbers are conditional. On RH-claims, Gershon (Preprints.org, 22 Apr 2026) and Pavesi (Zenodo, 23 Jun 2026) both claim RH and hence Λ = 0; I found no engagement with either, and the Gershon abstract itself confines a key sign condition to a verified range of degrees and indices. Close calls: (a) whether a bound from an unrefereed AI-assisted computation counts as movement, which the record gives as event data and does not decide; (b) whether Gomila's 'my own work' statement or the disclosure of AI exploration is the authoritative account of authorship; (c) which 2026 bound the problem's status rests on, which I have not chosen.
competing_reading: Read as a sequence of real progress, the 2026 claims narrow the window from [0, 0.2] to [0, 0.1493] (Raymond) in three months, with formal checks on several (Gordon's Lean layer, Murphy's kernel-checked 9/32, the Aristotle lemmas). On that reading the AI-involved claims (Gomila, Mosaic 'fully AI-derived', Raymond 'AI assistance', the OpenAI input to 9/32) are real mathematical movement, and the problem is no longer 'nothing happened'. The opposite reading is that none of these moves the value: every 2026 claim is unrefereed, most are conditional or 'audit-relative' in the authors' own words, the best-supported critique says there is 'no new mathematics', and the only human reviewer named (Romik) has not said anything public. On that reading the value is undetermined and the 2026 bounds are candidate endpoints only. A third reading: Gershon and Pavesi would close the problem if right, and neither has been engaged with at all.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Publication or public expert verdict on Gomila's package, specifically Dan Romik's own written statement and the referee's identity. (2) Named-expert review of Raymond's analytic reductions (the repo says these need human review) and of Gordon's conditional inputs. (3) Whether OpenAI's zero-free theorem is at 7/8 or 11/12 (the version history of openai/math), and whether it implies H(7/8). (4) The paper PDF of Mosaic's v2, to name the system behind 'fully AI-derived'. (5) Kornaus's primary paper, which I could not find. (6) Full text of Gershon's preprint (Preprints.org returned 403) and any expert comment on the 10,822-point interval step. (7) The rest of Planat's v2 (beyond the first 100,000 characters) to check the 0.157371 candidate and its 'not by itself a global upper bound' caveat. (8) Whether Gomila's 0.1787854 is cited by a later peer-reviewed paper, and whether the 0.1875 (Mosaic) is among its references.
